text:
**The Deep End**

In college, Q was the sort of person about whom other people said "Of course," as in: Of course he got the fellowship. Of course he'd been to Senegal. Of course he knew how to fix the radiator in our hallway, and of course, having fixed it, he made no speech about it, only wiped his hands on his jeans and asked whether anyone wanted tea. His real name was Quentin, but no one used it, because Q suited him: a single clean stroke, nothing extra.

I met him the second week of freshman year, in a stairwell of Hollis Hall that smelled of burnt popcorn and wet wool. I was sitting on the landing with a plate of dining-hall rice, having decided that I would rather eat alone in a stairwell than alone at a table. Q came down the steps two at a time, stopped, looked at me, and said, "That's the best idea anyone's had all week." Then he sat down next to me with his own plate. This was, I understood even then, a kind of genius: to make a person's loneliness feel like a position he had taken on purpose.

For four years I was in his orbit, though I hope I was a little more than a satellite. He read my terrible short stories and said true, specific things about them, never "I loved it" and never "It needs work," but "The father disappears on page four and you don't notice he's gone until page nine, and I think that's the best thing in it." He was the only person I knew who wrote thank-you notes by hand and could also stay up until four arguing about Rawls and still be at the pool by seven for swim practice. He swam the 200 butterfly, and seemed less to be fighting the water than to have reached an understanding with it.

I did not entirely like this about him. Admiration, over time, curdles into a low and private annoyance, like a tooth. I kept waiting for the flaw, the cruelty or vanity or secret cheating that would make him my size. It never came. When his girlfriend left him junior year, he sent her flowers on her birthday anyway. Even his heartbreak was well made.

After graduation, he went to New York, to a firm that did something with municipal bonds, and I went to Chicago for a master's I did not finish. We wrote for a year, then a few times a year, and then there was the email I never answered, in which he told me he was getting married and asked me to stand up with him. I think the reason was that I was thirty pounds heavier and unemployed, and the idea of standing next to him in a rented tuxedo, in photographs, forever, was more than I could bear. I told myself I'd write after the wedding, and then after the honeymoon, and then it was a decade.

---

I moved to Philadelphia for a job I won't describe, because it is the kind of job that makes people's eyes go flat. I joined the Y on Walnut Street because my doctor said "cholesterol" in a tone I recognized as a threat. I swam at six-thirty in the morning, when the pool belonged to the same dozen people: a retired judge in a paisley cap, two women who discussed their daughters-in-law, a man who wore a snorkel for reasons no one questioned.

It was a Thursday in March when I saw him. I was at the shallow end, hanging on the wall, catching my breath, wearing goggles and a silicone cap that made me look, my ex-wife once said, like a boiled egg. A man came out of the locker room and walked to the far edge of the pool, and something in the walk, the loose, unbothered length of it, made me go still.

He was heavier, but not much, in the way of someone who has been busy rather than careless, and there was a tiredness around the eyes I would not have predicted. But it was Q. He sat on the edge of the pool, lowered his feet into the water, and looked at it as though waiting for it to say something first.

I should have swum over. Any decent person would have pulled off the goggles and said his name. Instead I stayed where I was, in my egg-cap, and let the water close a little higher around my shoulders. Ten years of silence is a debt, and I did not have the cash.

I was still deciding when the woman arrived.

She came from the front desk in street clothes: a camel coat, a leather bag, boots that clicked on the wet tile. She was perhaps forty, with a sharp, intelligent face and the posture of someone who has been underestimated. She stopped beside Q and said, "They told me you'd be here."

Q looked up. I watched his face do something I had never seen it do, which was to arrange itself. In college his expressions had simply happened, like weather. Now there was a half second of construction, a pleasant mask being lowered into place. "Marianne," he said. "Hi. Did we have a meeting?"

"We were supposed to," she said. "Yesterday. At four."

"Right," said Q. "God. I'm so sorry. It was one of those days."

Sound travels over water as though along a wire; I heard every word. I hung on the wall and tried to look like a man concentrating on his breathing.

"I wanted to talk to you about the Lisbon project," Marianne said.

"Yes."

"Because I heard something. From Greg. And I thought I'd rather hear it from you."

Here, I thought, was where Q would be Q: the clean, kind, true thing, absorbed with grace.

"So," Q said. He moved his feet in the water. "There's been some discussion. About resourcing. And the timeline's shifted, and I think the feeling is that, at this stage, it might make sense to look at the structure of the team, in a way that—" He paused. "It's not about performance. I want to say that clearly."

"Okay," said Marianne. "So am I on it or not?"

"I think," Q said, "that what we want to do is stay flexible."

There was a silence. In the next lane the man with the snorkel passed, exhaling bubbles like a small, aggrieved engine.

"Quentin," she said. I had not heard anyone say his full name in ten years. "Is that a no?"

"It's not a no."

"Is it a yes?"

"It's—" He laughed, and it was a terrible laugh, high and apologetic. "It's a 'let's talk Monday.'"

"Greg already told me," Marianne said, not unkindly. "He said the decision was made two weeks ago. He said you'd be the one to tell me. I've been waiting two weeks."

I felt, watching him, a sensation I can only describe as vertigo. It was not triumph. I had imagined triumph, over the years, in the small mean hours, and what I felt instead was closer to the feeling of seeing your father cry.

"I wanted to find the right way," he said finally, and his voice cracked. "I kept thinking there'd be a way to say it that wouldn't—" He stopped. "I'm not very good at this part. I know people think I am."

Marianne looked at him for a long moment. She seemed, if anything, a little sorry for him, which I think was the worst of it. "I know," she said. "You'd make a lovely person to be fired by."

"You're not being fired."

"No," she said. "Just flexible."

She adjusted the strap of her bag, said she would see him Monday, and walked back toward the front desk, her boots leaving small dark prints that the tile dried almost at once. Q sat for some time without moving. Then he slid into the water, with none of his old ease, and began to swim, not butterfly but a plain, graceless freestyle, his head too high, his kick too wide. He swam like a man trying to outrun a sentence.

He did four laps. On the fifth he stopped at the wall near me, breathing hard, three feet away. He pushed his goggles up and looked straight at me. I braced myself.

"Morning," he said, with a small, tired nod.

"Morning," I said, in a voice an octave lower than my own.

There was no recognition. He saw an egg-headed stranger, a fellow sufferer of the early shift, and pushed off again.

On the walk to the office I took out my phone and found his name, still there between a dentist and a man named Quincy who once fixed my car. I typed: *I owe you an answer to an email. It's a long one. I'm sorry.* Then I added, because it was true, *I saw you at the pool today. You looked like you could use a friend who's bad at things too.*

I deleted the second sentence. I sent the first.
